conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What is tonsillitis, and why is it an antibiotic-stewardship topic?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Acute inflammation of the tonsils (usually the palatine tonsils) — a common cause of sore throat. Most cases are viral and self-limiting; a minority are bacterial (Group A Strep) with risks of suppurative (quinsy) and non-suppurative (rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis) sequelae. The Centor and FeverPAIN scores exist to decide who needs antibiotics.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What are the causes of tonsillitis?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Mostly viral (adenovirus, rhinovirus, EBV, etc.). Bacterial: Group A Streptococcus (Strep pyogenes) is the important one (→ penicillin V); also Strep pneumoniae. The palatine tonsils are usually infected.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: How does infectious mononucleosis (EBV) present differently from bacterial tonsillitis, and what antibiotic must be avoided?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: EBV: exudative tonsillitis + GENERALISED lymphadenopathy + splenomegaly (bacterial has anterior cervical nodes only). Amoxicillin causes a rash in EBV, so it must be avoided.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What are the clinical features of tonsillitis?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Sore throat, pain on swallowing (odynophagia), fever, neck pain, referred ear pain, and swollen tender lymph nodes. On exam: red, inflamed, enlarged tonsils ± exudate; anterior cervical lymphadenopathy.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What are the Centor criteria, and what score prompts antibiotics?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: One point each: Fever >38°C; tonsillar Exudate; Absence of cough; tender Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Antibiotics if ≥3 (predicts a streptococcal cause).

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What are the FeverPAIN score components, and what score prompts antibiotics?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: One point each (applies to any sore throat): Fever (>38, last 24 h); Purulence (exudate); Attend rapidly (≤3 days of onset); Inflamed tonsils (severe); No cough or coryza. Antibiotics if ≥4.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What does a LOW Centor/FeverPAIN score indicate for management?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: FeverPAIN 0–1 / Centor 0–2 → low likelihood of strep → no antibiotic, self-care + safety-net.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What does a MODERATE FeverPAIN score indicate?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: FeverPAIN 2–3 → moderate → a delayed ('back-up') prescription.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What does a HIGH Centor/FeverPAIN score indicate?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: FeverPAIN 4–5 / Centor 3–4 → high likelihood (~62%) → immediate antibiotic.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: When should a patient with tonsillitis be considered for admission?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: If immunocompromised, systemically unwell, dehydrated, has stridor/respiratory distress, or has evidence of a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)/cellulitis.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What is the management of viral/low-score tonsillitis?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Simple analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen) and fluids; safety-net — return if not resolving after 3 days or fever >38.3.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What is the first-line antibiotic for tonsillitis, and the duration?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) for 5–10 days (when Centor ≥3 or FeverPAIN ≥4).

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What antibiotic is used for tonsillitis in penicillin allergy, and which is avoided?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Penicillin allergy → clarithromycin (erythromycin in pregnancy). Avoid amoxicillin (rash if EBV).

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What are the SUPPURATIVE complications of tonsillitis?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess), otitis media, parapharyngeal/retropharyngeal abscess, and Lemierre's syndrome.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What are the NON-SUPPURATIVE (post-streptococcal) complications of tonsillitis?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Scarlet fever, rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and reactive arthritis.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What is quinsy (peritonsillar abscess)?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: A collection of pus in the peritonsillar space (between the tonsil capsule and the pharyngeal muscles) — usually a complication of (untreated) tonsillitis but can occur alone. Mostly Strep pyogenes (Group A), often polymicrobial. It is an ENT emergency.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What are the red-flag additional signs of quinsy beyond tonsillitis?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Trismus (can't open the mouth — pterygoid irritation), a 'hot potato'/muffled voice (pharyngeal swelling), swelling + erythema beside the tonsil with the tonsil pushed medially, uvula deviated to the unaffected side, drooling, unilateral pain, and halitosis.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: Which way does the uvula deviate in quinsy?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Away from the abscess (to the unaffected side).

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What is the management of quinsy?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Urgent ENT review; drainage (needle aspiration OR incision and drainage); IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. co-amoxiclav per local guidance); analgesia and IV fluids; a single dose of corticosteroid (dexamethasone) may reduce symptoms. Interval tonsillectomy may be considered after recurrent quinsy.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What are the Paradise/SIGN indications for tonsillectomy in recurrent tonsillitis?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: ≥7 episodes in 1 year, OR ≥5/year for 2 years, OR ≥3/year for 3 years.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: Besides recurrent tonsillitis, what are the other indications for tonsillectomy?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Recurrent tonsillar abscesses (≥2 episodes of quinsy); and enlarged tonsils causing obstruction — difficulty breathing/swallowing, obstructive sleep apnoea, snoring.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: How is tonsillectomy performed, and what are the general complications?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Under general anaesthesia, usually as a day case. Complications: sore throat ~2 weeks, dental damage, infection, anaesthetic risks, and post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What is PRIMARY (reactionary) post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage and its management?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Bleeding within 24 hours (typically the first 6–8 hours) → immediate return to theatre.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: What is SECONDARY post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage and its management?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Bleeding 5–10 days post-op, associated with wound infection → antibiotics + admit.

conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.front: Why is post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage potentially life-threatening?
conditions__ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy.back: Because of the risk of aspiration of blood (and significant blood loss) — it is an emergency.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the organising principle for rhinitis, sinusitis and nasal polyps?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Allergic vs infective vs chronic inflammatory: allergic rhinitis (sneezing, itch, clear rhinorrhoea, atopy) vs sinusitis (facial pain/pressure, purulent discharge, mostly viral) vs chronic rhinosinusitis ± polyps.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What features of a nasal polyp or discharge should prompt referral to exclude malignancy?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: A unilateral nasal polyp or bloody discharge.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is Samter's triad?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Aspirin-sensitive asthma + nasal polyps + aspirin/NSAID sensitivity (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is allergic rhinitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: IgE-mediated inflammation of the nasal mucosa triggered by allergen exposure — the nasal counterpart of allergic conjunctivitis and the 'R' of the atopic march. It is extremely common ('hay fever') and frequently coexists with asthma/conjunctivitis ('one airway').

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the mechanism of allergic rhinitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Allergen (pollen, dust mite, dander) binds IgE on nasal mast cells → degranulation → histamine + mediators → sneezing, itch, rhinorrhoea, congestion. Early phase (histamine — sneeze/itch/watery discharge) + late phase (cellular infiltrate — congestion).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: How is allergic rhinitis classified?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Seasonal (pollen — 'hay fever') vs perennial (house dust mite, dander, mould); or intermittent vs persistent (ARIA); and mild vs moderate–severe (by impact).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What are the clinical features of allergic rhinitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Sneezing, nasal itch, watery rhinorrhoea, congestion/blockage; itchy watery eyes; itchy palate/throat; postnasal drip, reduced smell, mouth breathing/snoring; and associated atopy. On exam: pale, boggy, oedematous nasal mucosa with clear discharge; in children the 'allergic salute'/nasal crease and allergic shiners.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: How is allergic rhinitis diagnosed and when is allergy testing done?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Clinical diagnosis (history + exam). Skin-prick testing or specific IgE (RAST) if the trigger is unclear or immunotherapy is considered.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the stepwise management ladder for allergic rhinitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: (1) Allergen avoidance + nasal saline irrigation; (2) antihistamines (oral non-sedating cetirizine/loratadine/fexofenadine, or intranasal azelastine) for mild/intermittent; (3) intranasal corticosteroids — the most effective single agent, first-line for moderate–severe/persistent; (4) combination intranasal steroid + antihistamine; (5) add-ons — montelukast (esp. with asthma), short oral steroid for flares; (6) allergen immunotherapy for refractory disease.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the most effective single agent for allergic rhinitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Intranasal corticosteroids (fluticasone, mometasone, beclometasone) — first-line for moderate–severe/persistent symptoms, and they treat congestion too.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: Which allergic rhinitis symptoms respond well to antihistamines, and which less so?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Antihistamines are good for sneeze/itch/rhinorrhoea, but less effective for congestion (for which intranasal steroids are better).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is rhinitis medicamentosa and how is it avoided?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Rebound congestion from prolonged use of topical decongestants (oxymetazoline) — avoid using them beyond 5–7 days.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: When is a leukotriene receptor antagonist (montelukast) particularly useful in allergic rhinitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: As an add-on, especially in patients with coexisting asthma.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is rhinosinusitis, and why is 'rhino-' included?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Inflammation of the paranasal sinuses — correctly called rhinosinusitis because the nose is always involved.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the mechanism of sinusitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Sinuses produce mucus that drains into the nasal cavity via the ostia. Blockage of the ostia (mucosal swelling after a viral URTI, allergy, polyps, foreign body, trauma) → disrupted drainage → mucus stagnation → inflammation/infection.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: How do acute and chronic rhinosinusitis differ in duration and cause?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Acute: <12 weeks (usually resolves in 2–3 weeks), mostly viral (post-URTI, minority bacterial). Chronic (CRS): ≥12 weeks, persistent inflammation ± nasal polyps.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What bacteria cause bacterial acute sinusitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What are the clinical features of acute sinusitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: After a recent viral URTI: nasal congestion + discharge; facial pain/pressure/headache worse on bending forward; swelling/tenderness over the sinus; cough (postnasal drip); and reduced smell.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the characteristic facial pain of sinusitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Facial pain/pressure that is worse on bending forward.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: When is imaging needed in sinusitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Most acute cases need NO investigation (clinical). If persistent despite management → nasal endoscopy + CT sinuses (CT is the imaging of choice for CRS).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What are the red flags in sinusitis that warrant ENT referral to exclude a tumour?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Unilateral symptoms, persistence despite 3 months of management, and epistaxis (exclude nasopharyngeal/sinonasal carcinoma).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the management of acute sinusitis with symptoms of 10 days or less (NICE NG79)?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: No antibiotics (mostly viral, resolve in 2–3 weeks) — analgesia ± a short decongestant. (Systemic infection/sepsis → admit.)

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the management of acute sinusitis with symptoms lasting MORE than 10 days and not improving?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: High-dose intranasal corticosteroid for 14 days (e.g. mometasone 200 mcg BD, ≥12 years); a back-up (delayed) antibiotic — phenoxymethylpenicillin for 5 days — if worsening/no improvement in ~7 days (especially 'double-sickening'); immediate co-amoxiclav if very unwell.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is 'double-sickening' in sinusitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: An initial viral illness that improves, then worsens again — suggesting secondary bacterial infection, and prompting consideration of antibiotics.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: How is chronic rhinosinusitis managed?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Allergen avoidance; long-term intranasal corticosteroids; saline nasal irrigation; treat contributing factors (allergy, smoking cessation); ± short oral steroids (especially polyps); and ENT referral/FESS if refractory.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What are the complications of sinusitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Orbital/periorbital cellulitis (from the ethmoid sinus → eye swelling, painful/restricted eye movements, proptosis, visual change — an emergency); intracranial spread (meningitis, abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis); osteomyelitis of the frontal bone (Pott's puffy tumour); and mucocele.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS)?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Persistent inflammation of the nasal and paranasal sinus mucosa lasting ≥12 weeks (~10% of the population). It is now organised by phenotype — with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) vs without (CRSsNP) — because this drives treatment.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the mechanism of chronic rhinosinusitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Persistent mucosal inflammation + impaired mucociliary clearance + ostial obstruction → a self-perpetuating cycle of stasis, inflammation and (often) infection, driven by dysregulated immune responses (frequently type 2/eosinophilic, especially with polyps).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What are the EPOS diagnostic criteria for CRS?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: ≥12 weeks of ≥2 symptoms, one of which must be nasal blockage/obstruction/congestion OR nasal discharge, ± facial pain/pressure and/or reduction/loss of smell — PLUS objective evidence (endoscopic signs — polyps, mucopurulent discharge, or oedema/obstruction in the middle meatus — or CT changes in the ostiomeatal complex/sinuses).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What distinguishes CRS with polyps (CRSwNP) from CRS without polyps (CRSsNP)?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: CRSwNP: bilateral polyps on endoscopy, usually type 2/eosinophilic inflammation, associated with asthma/aspirin sensitivity (Samter's) and allergy, prominent anosmia, and responsive to biologics (dupilumab). CRSsNP: no polyps, more variable/neutrophilic inflammation, associated with prior infection/anatomical/ciliary factors, less anosmia, less applicable to biologics.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What are the predisposing factors for chronic rhinosinusitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Atopy/allergy, nasal obstruction (deviated septum, polyps), recent/recurrent local infection, swimming, smoking; and asthma, aspirin sensitivity, cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, and immunodeficiency (especially young/bilateral polyps).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What should young patients with bilateral nasal polyps be investigated for?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Cystic fibrosis / ciliary function testing (primary ciliary dyskinesia).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What are the clinical features of chronic rhinosinusitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Facial pain/pressure worse on bending forward; nasal discharge (anterior/postnasal drip); obstruction/congestion → mouth breathing; postnasal drip → chronic cough; reduced/lost smell (especially polyps). Systemic upset/fever is uncommon (suggests exacerbation/complication).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What are the investigations for chronic rhinosinusitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Nasal endoscopy (polyps, discharge, middle-meatus oedema/obstruction) and CT sinuses (imaging of choice — extent of mucosal disease, ostiomeatal complex, essential for surgical planning). Consider allergy testing; CF/ciliary testing if young + bilateral polyps.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the conservative management of chronic rhinosinusitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Allergen avoidance + manage contributing factors (smoking cessation, treat allergy/asthma); intranasal corticosteroids (mainstay — sprays, or drops/rinses for polyps); and high-volume saline irrigation.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What are the escalation and surgical options for chronic rhinosinusitis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Escalation: a short course of oral corticosteroids (significant polyps/severe symptoms); treat bacterial exacerbations; long-term low-dose macrolides sometimes in CRSsNP. Surgical: functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) for disease refractory to maximal medical therapy (polyps recur in a substantial proportion).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What biologics are used for severe CRS with nasal polyps, and which has transformed care?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Dupilumab (anti-IL-4/13), omalizumab (anti-IgE), and mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) — for severe uncontrolled CRSwNP despite medical therapy ± surgery. Dupilumab has transformed severe CRSwNP care.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What are nasal polyps?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Benign, oedematous swellings of the nasal/sinus mucosa that grow into the nasal cavity. They define CRS with nasal polyps (CRSwNP), cause troublesome nasal obstruction and anosmia, and link to systemic associations (asthma, aspirin sensitivity, cystic fibrosis).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the single most important rule about nasal polyps?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Bilateral polyps are benign and GP-managed; a UNILATERAL polyp is a red flag for malignancy.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the mechanism of nasal polyp formation?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: They arise from chronic inflammation of the sinonasal mucosa — usually type 2 (Th2/eosinophilic) inflammation → mucosal oedema that prolapses into the nasal cavity as pale, grape-like swellings that grow slowly and gradually obstruct.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What are the systemic associations of nasal polyps?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Chronic rhinosinusitis (polyps define CRSwNP), asthma, cystic fibrosis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss), Samter's triad (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease), allergic rhinitis and chronic infection.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: Why do nasal polyps in a child/young patient warrant investigation for cystic fibrosis?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Because polyps are rare in children, so their presence is a red flag — consider cystic fibrosis (and primary ciliary dyskinesia).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is Samter's triad?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD): nasal polyps + asthma + aspirin/NSAID sensitivity.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What are the clinical features of nasal polyps?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Usually bilateral, with symptoms of chronic rhinosinusitis: nasal obstruction (difficulty breathing through the nose), snoring, nasal discharge/rhinorrhoea/postnasal drip, and loss of sense of smell (anosmia/hyposmia — a cardinal feature).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the cardinal symptom of nasal polyps?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Loss of sense of smell (anosmia/hyposmia).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What do nasal polyps look and feel like on examination?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Pale/grey, mobile, insensate swellings — touching a polyp doesn't hurt (unlike the very sensate turbinate).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: How can a polyp be distinguished from a turbinate on examination?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: A polyp is pale, mobile and insensate (touching it doesn't hurt), whereas the turbinate is very sensate (touching it is painful).

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What investigations are used for nasal polyps?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Anterior rhinoscopy with a nasal speculum; nasal endoscopy (specialist — better visualisation); CT sinuses (extent/surgical planning, and to assess a mass if unilateral/atypical); consider CF testing in young patients and allergy/asthma assessment.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: How does management differ between bilateral and unilateral nasal polyps?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Bilateral: benign (CRSwNP) → GP management with intranasal steroids. Unilateral: RED FLAG → urgent ENT referral to exclude malignancy (± biopsy), before any treatment.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the differential for a unilateral nasal polyp/mass?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Sinonasal SCC, inverted papilloma, esthesioneuroblastoma, antrochoanal polyp, and fungal sinusitis.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What features with a unilateral polyp especially suggest a tumour?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Epistaxis, facial pain/swelling, visual change, or cranial nerve signs — a unilateral polyp is a tumour until proven otherwise → urgent ENT referral for endoscopy ± biopsy and imaging.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What is the first-line treatment for bilateral nasal polyps?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Intranasal topical corticosteroid — drops or spray (long-term); drops are often preferred for larger/higher polyps (better penetration). Nasal saline irrigation is an adjunct.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: Why are intranasal steroid DROPS often preferred over spray for larger/higher nasal polyps?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Because drops give better penetration to reach larger or higher polyps.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: When and how are oral corticosteroids used for nasal polyps?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: A short course (prednisolone ~2 weeks) for significant polyps/severe symptoms — it shrinks polyps, is used sparingly, and repeated no more than about twice a year.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What surgical options exist for nasal polyps, and what is the caveat?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: If medical treatment fails: intranasal polypectomy (polyps near the nostrils) or endoscopic polypectomy/FESS (further back). Polyps commonly recur (especially in AERD), so continue steroids/saline post-op.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: What treatments are used for severe/recurrent nasal polyps?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Aspirin desensitisation for AERD/Samter's; and biologics — dupilumab, omalizumab, mepolizumab — for severe uncontrolled CRSwNP.

conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.front: Are nasal polyps usually unilateral or bilateral, and why does this matter?
conditions__ENT__Rhinitis, Sinusitis & N.back: Usually bilateral (benign CRSwNP, GP-managed). A unilateral polyp is the exception and is a red flag for malignancy requiring urgent ENT referral.

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: What is Ramsay Hunt syndrome (RHS)?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: A facial nerve palsy caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve, producing the triad of ear pain, a vesicular rash, and lower-motor-neuron facial weakness.

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: How common is Ramsay Hunt, and how does its prognosis compare with Bell's palsy?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: It is the second commonest cause of atraumatic facial palsy (after Bell's palsy) and has a WORSE prognosis than Bell's — early antiviral + steroid treatment (within 72 hours) substantially improves recovery.

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: What is the core one-line message for Ramsay Hunt?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Facial palsy + vesicles around the ear = Ramsay Hunt (not Bell's) → aciclovir + steroids.

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: What is the core mechanism of Ramsay Hunt?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: After chickenpox, VZV lies dormant in sensory ganglia. It reactivates in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve (CN VII) → inflammation + oedema of the nerve in its bony canal → LMN facial weakness, plus a vesicular zoster rash in the nerve's sensory territory (the ear).

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: Why are vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss common in Ramsay Hunt?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Because CN VIII runs alongside CN VII in the internal acoustic meatus, so it is often affected too.

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: What is the classic triad of Ramsay Hunt?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Ear pain (otalgia) + a vesicular rash (ear/canal/palate) + lower-motor-neuron facial weakness.

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: How does Ramsay Hunt differ from Bell's palsy?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Both cause LMN facial palsy (forehead involved). RHS: VZV reactivation, vesicular rash (ear/canal/palate), severe otalgia (often precedes rash), common CN VIII symptoms (vertigo/tinnitus/hearing loss), worse prognosis, treat with antiviral + steroid. Bell's: idiopathic (?HSV), no rash, mild/no pain, uncommon CN VIII symptoms, better prognosis, steroid (± antiviral).

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: Why is the forehead affected in Ramsay Hunt, and what would spare it?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Because it is a LOWER motor neuron palsy → the forehead IS affected (can't wrinkle the forehead/raise the eyebrow on the affected side). An UPPER motor neuron lesion (e.g. stroke) SPARES the forehead — a key distinction.

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: What is often the FIRST symptom of Ramsay Hunt?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Auricular pain (otalgia) — it may precede the rash.

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: Describe the facial palsy in Ramsay Hunt.
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Unilateral LMN weakness — drooping mouth, inability to close the eye, and loss of forehead wrinkling on the affected side.

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: Where is the vesicular rash in Ramsay Hunt?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Around the ear (pinna, external auditory canal); it may involve the tympanic membrane, palate, or anterior tongue.

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: What other CN VII-related features can occur in Ramsay Hunt?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Loss of taste (anterior 2/3 tongue), reduced lacrimation/dry eye, and hyperacusis (branches of CN VII).

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: What is 'zoster sine herpete' in the context of Ramsay Hunt?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: When the rash follows, or is absent — the facial palsy can precede visible vesicles. VZV PCR helps confirm the diagnosis in these cases.

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: How is Ramsay Hunt diagnosed?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Primarily a clinical diagnosis (facial palsy + vesicular rash in the ear). VZV PCR (from vesicle swab/ear exudate) can confirm — useful to distinguish zoster sine herpete from Bell's palsy. MRI if atypical/polycranial/diagnostic doubt; pure-tone audiometry if hearing affected.

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: What is the key timing rule for treating Ramsay Hunt?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Start treatment as early as possible — ideally within 72 hours of symptom onset (recovery rates are much higher with early treatment).

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: What is the antiviral treatment for Ramsay Hunt?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Oral aciclovir (e.g. 800 mg five times daily for 7 days; or valaciclovir/famciclovir).

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: What is added to the antiviral in Ramsay Hunt, and why?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Oral corticosteroids (prednisolone) — to reduce nerve inflammation/oedema.

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: What eye care is essential in Ramsay Hunt, and why?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: If the eye won't close, protect the cornea — lubricating drops, ointment at night, taping the eye closed — to prevent exposure keratopathy/corneal ulceration.

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: What symptomatic treatments are used in Ramsay Hunt?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Analgesia (neuropathic pain is often significant); antiemetics/vestibular sedatives for vertigo; and treatment of any post-herpetic neuralgia (amitriptyline/gabapentin).

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: What is the prognosis of Ramsay Hunt?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Worse than Bell's palsy — complete recovery is less likely, especially if treatment is delayed beyond 72 hours or the initial palsy is severe (higher House-Brackmann grade).

conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.front: What are the possible sequelae of Ramsay Hunt?
conditions__ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome.back: Incomplete facial recovery, synkinesis (involuntary co-movement), and persistent hearing loss/tinnitus/vertigo.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What does 'otitis' (ear infections) cover, and what is the organising principle?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Infection/inflammation of the ear — the external canal (otitis externa) and the middle ear (otitis media, acute and with effusion). Mostly clinical diagnoses on otoscopy. The organising principle is to localise the problem: canal (OE — pain on moving the tragus/pinna, discharge) vs middle ear behind an intact drum (AOM — bulging red drum; glue ear — retracted dull drum + effusion).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is malignant otitis externa and who gets it?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: A dangerous skull-base extension (osteomyelitis) in diabetics/immunocompromised — an emergency: severe unremitting otalgia + granulation tissue → urgent ENT + IV antibiotics + imaging.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is otitis media with effusion (glue ear) and why does it matter?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: A dull retracted drum with a middle-ear effusion causing conductive hearing loss — the commonest cause of childhood hearing loss, which can impair speech/development; grommets if persistent.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is acute otitis media (AOM)?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Acute infection/inflammation of the middle ear (the air-filled space behind the tympanic membrane housing the ossicles) — one of the commonest infections of childhood (the classic 'child with ear pain after a cold'). Most are self-limiting.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the core mechanism of AOM?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: A viral URTI → Eustachian tube dysfunction/oedema → the middle ear can't drain/ventilate → bacteria ascend from the nasopharynx → infection with pus under pressure. This is why AOM follows a cold.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: Why are children particularly prone to AOM?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Because they have short, horizontal Eustachian tubes, which drain/ventilate the middle ear less effectively.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What organisms cause AOM?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Often preceded by a viral URTI; the commonest bacteria are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae (also Moraxella catarrhalis).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What are the clinical features of AOM?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Otalgia (infants/young children may rub or tug at the ear, be irritable, feed poorly, or have fever); reduced (conductive) hearing in the affected ear; preceding URTI symptoms (cough, coryza, sore throat); and vertigo/balance problems if the vestibular system is involved.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What happens if the tympanic membrane perforates in AOM?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Discharge (otorrhoea) occurs, often with sudden relief of pain (the pressure is released).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What does a NORMAL tympanic membrane look like on otoscopy?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Pearly grey, translucent, slightly shiny, with a light reflex.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What are the otoscopy findings of AOM?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: A bulging tympanic membrane with loss of the light reflex (the hallmark); erythema and opacification of the TM; loss of the normal landmarks (malleus handle obscured); a perforation with purulent discharge if ruptured; and an air-fluid level/bubbles behind the drum.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the hallmark otoscopy finding of AOM?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: A bulging tympanic membrane with loss of the light reflex.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the mainstay of management for AOM, and the natural course?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Most cases resolve without antibiotics (symptoms usually settle within ~3 days; ~60% improve within 24 h), so analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen) is the mainstay.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: When is NO antibiotic (with safety-netting) appropriate for AOM?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Most children >2 years, with unilateral AOM, who are not systemically unwell.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: When is a delayed ('back-up') antibiotic prescription used in AOM?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: To be started after 3 days if symptoms haven't improved or have worsened.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: When is an IMMEDIATE antibiotic indicated in AOM?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: If systemically unwell; significant comorbidity; immunocompromised; <2 years with BILATERAL AOM; or otorrhoea/perforation.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the first-line antibiotic for AOM, and the mnemonic?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Amoxicillin for 5–7 days ('Acute Otitis Media → AMoxicillin').

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What antibiotics are used in AOM for penicillin allergy, in pregnancy, and second-line?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin. Pregnancy (if a macrolide is needed): erythromycin. Second-line/treatment failure: co-amoxiclav.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What safety-netting advice is given for AOM?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Return if symptoms worsen rapidly, don't improve in 3 days, discharge begins, or the child becomes systemically very unwell. Admit/urgent referral if severe systemic infection or a suspected complication (mastoiditis, meningitis, intracranial abscess, facial palsy).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM)?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: When a perforation with discharge persists for >6 weeks after AOM.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is mastoiditis and how does it present?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Spread of AOM to the mastoid air cells → postauricular swelling/erythema/tenderness, a protruding auricle, and systemic illness → IV antibiotics ± mastoidectomy.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What are the intracranial complications of AOM?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Rare but life-threatening: meningitis, intracranial/extradural abscess, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST), and facial nerve palsy.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What are the other/local complications of AOM?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Tympanic membrane perforation → otorrhoea (usually heals); conductive hearing loss (usually temporary); labyrinthitis (→ vertigo); glue ear (persistent middle-ear effusion → conductive loss); and cholesteatoma (with chronic disease).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Inflammation of the skin of the external auditory canal (the 'outer' ear infection, aka 'swimmer's ear'). It is common and usually simple — treated with topical drops, not oral antibiotics — but must be distinguished from otitis media and from the rare life-threatening variant, malignant (necrotising) otitis externa.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the core mechanism of otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: The ear canal is normally protected by cerumen (acidic, water-repellent) and intact skin. Anything that breaches this — water (raises pH, macerates skin), trauma (cotton buds), or wax removal — lets bacteria/fungi invade the canal skin. So the risk factors are all things that damage the canal's defences.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What are the commonest organisms in otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus; fungal (Candida/Aspergillus — otomycosis) especially after multiple courses of topical antibiotics.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What are the risk factors for otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Swimming/water exposure ('swimmer's ear' — moisture macerates the canal); trauma to the canal (cotton buds, earplugs, hearing aids); multiple courses of topical antibiotics (→ fungal superinfection); eczema/psoriasis/seborrhoeic dermatitis of the canal; a narrow canal; and diabetes/immunocompromise.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the distinguishing symptom of otitis externa versus otitis media?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Ear pain that is worse on moving the tragus/pinna (or inserting an otoscope) — pointing to the canal (OE) rather than the middle ear (OM).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What are the clinical features of otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Ear pain (worse on tragus/pinna movement), prominent itch (especially fungal), discharge (otorrhoea), conductive hearing loss if the canal occludes; on examination erythema + swelling of the canal, tenderness, pus/discharge/debris, regional lymphadenopathy, and the TM may be obscured (try to visualise it to exclude perforation/OM).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the general management of simple otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen); aural toilet (microsuction/cleaning of debris to improve drop penetration — a key, often-overlooked step); and topical antibiotic ± corticosteroid ear drops as the mainstay (typically 7 days).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: Why is aural toilet an important step in otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Microsuction/cleaning of debris improves penetration of the topical drops — a key, often-overlooked step.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What are examples of topical drops for otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Topical antibiotic ± corticosteroid — e.g. ciprofloxacin + dexamethasone, or gentamicin/neomycin + steroid, typically for 7 days.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: Which topical drops must be avoided if the tympanic membrane is perforated, and why?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Aminoglycoside drops (gentamicin/neomycin) — because of ototoxicity risk. Use a non-ototoxic agent (e.g. ciprofloxacin) instead.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: How is fungal otitis externa (otomycosis) treated?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: A topical antifungal (e.g. clotrimazole); acetic acid 2% spray for mild cases.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What self-care advice is given in otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Keep the ear dry, avoid cotton buds; an ear swab is taken if resistant/recurrent.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: Are oral antibiotics routinely needed in otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: No — topical treatment is superior and oral antibiotics are NOT routinely needed. Reserve them for spreading infection/cellulitis, systemic illness, or diabetes/immunocompromise.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: How does simple OE differ from malignant (necrotising) OE?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Simple OE: anyone (swimmers, trauma), Pseudomonas/Staph/fungal, moderate pain, red swollen canal, confined to canal skin, topical drops. Malignant OE: elderly diabetics/immunocompromised, Pseudomonas (>90%), severe disproportionate unremitting pain (worse at night), granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction, skull-base osteomyelitis → cranial nerve palsies (facial first), needs CT/MRI + IV ciprofloxacin.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the key examination sign that should raise concern for malignant otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Granulation tissue (classically at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the canal), especially with severe disproportionate unremitting pain in a diabetic/immunocompromised patient.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: When should you urgently refer suspected malignant otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Severe/unresolving OE with disproportionate pain, especially in a diabetic/immunocompromised patient (± granulation tissue/cranial nerve signs) → urgent ENT referral/admission.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What organism is the key pathogen in both swimmer's ear and malignant otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What complications can otitis externa lead to?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Spreading infection/cellulitis (perichondritis of the pinna), canal stenosis with chronic OE, fungal superinfection, and — the dangerous one — malignant (necrotising) otitis externa in at-risk patients.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is malignant (necrotising) otitis externa (MOE/NOE)?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: A rare, aggressive, potentially fatal infection in which otitis externa spreads from the ear canal into the temporal bone and skull base, causing osteomyelitis. It is a must-not-miss ENT emergency, almost exclusively in elderly diabetics and the immunocompromised.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: Why is it called 'malignant' if it is not a cancer?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: 'Malignant' reflects its aggressive, destructive behaviour — it is NOT a cancer. 'Necrotising otitis externa' is the more accurate name.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the core mechanism of malignant otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Infection (almost always Pseudomonas aeruginosa) starts in the external canal and spreads through the osseocartilaginous junction and fissures of Santorini into the skull base → progressive osteomyelitis. As it advances it reaches the cranial nerve foramina → cranial neuropathies (facial nerve first).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: Why are diabetics and the immunocompromised uniquely vulnerable to MOE?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Diabetic microvascular disease and impaired immunity make this population uniquely vulnerable to the infection spreading and progressing to skull-base osteomyelitis.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the red-flag triad for malignant otitis externa?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Elderly diabetic + severe pain out of proportion (worse at night) + granulation tissue in the canal = MOE until proven otherwise.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the dominant risk factor for MOE?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Diabetes mellitus (especially poorly controlled) — the classic and dominant risk factor.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: List the risk factors for MOE.
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Diabetes mellitus (dominant), immunocompromise (HIV, chemotherapy, immunosuppressants, elderly), preceding otitis externa (± ear syringing/trauma in a diabetic), and older age.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What organism causes >90% of MOE cases?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Pseudomonas aeruginosa. (Occasionally Staph aureus including MRSA; rarely fungal — Aspergillus/Candida — consider if not responding, especially if profoundly immunocompromised.)

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What are the clinical features of MOE?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Severe, deep, unremitting otalgia (worse at night, out of proportion to otoscopy); persistent otorrhoea not settling with topical treatment; granulation tissue in the canal (the hallmark); headache, temporomandibular/periauricular pain, pain on chewing; and variable systemic fever/malaise.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the hallmark examination sign of MOE, and where is it classically found?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Granulation tissue in the canal — classically at the bony-cartilaginous (osseocartilaginous) junction on the floor of the canal.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: Which cranial nerve is affected first and most commonly in MOE, and then which others?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: The facial nerve (CN VII) first and commonest (through the temporal bone), then IX, X, XI (jugular foramen syndrome) as it advances.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What blood tests are used in MOE and their role?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Raised inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR, WCC — ESR/CRP used to monitor response) and glucose/HbA1c (often poorly controlled diabetes).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the role of microbiology (swab/biopsy) in MOE?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Ear swab/canal biopsy for culture + sensitivities — essential to guide antibiotics (detect ciprofloxacin-resistant Pseudomonas); and biopsy of the granulation tissue to exclude malignancy (SCC).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What imaging is used in MOE?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: CT of the temporal bones (first-line — bony erosion/skull-base osteomyelitis + extent); MRI (best for soft-tissue + intracranial extension; used to monitor); and radionuclide scans (technetium-99m bone scan — sensitive but non-specific; gallium-67 — tracks active infection, monitors resolution and guides duration).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the first-line imaging in MOE, and what is best for intracranial extension?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: CT of the temporal bones is first-line (bony erosion). MRI is best for soft-tissue and intracranial extension.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the mainstay of treatment for MOE?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Urgent ENT referral/admission and prolonged IV antipseudomonal antibiotics — ciprofloxacin (± an antipseudomonal beta-lactam e.g. ceftazidime/piperacillin-tazobactam), culture-guided, typically ~6 weeks (up to ~3 months), guided by inflammatory markers and gallium scanning ('cipro moe the lawn').

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What resistance issue must be watched for in MOE, and how is it managed?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Ciprofloxacin-resistant Pseudomonas → adjust to sensitivities (e.g. ceftazidime). This is a currency point.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What non-antibiotic measures are central to MOE recovery?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Strict glycaemic control and correcting immunosuppression where possible; plus aural toilet/debridement.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the role of surgery in MOE?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Surgical debridement is reserved for granulation tissue/sequestra or non-response — surgery is NOT the mainstay (antibiotics are). Hyperbaric oxygen is used in refractory cases.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What team and follow-up does MOE require?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: MDT care (ENT, microbiology/ID, endocrinology ± ophthalmology/neurology) and long-term follow-up (recurrence is recognised).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What are the complications of MOE?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Skull-base osteomyelitis (the defining process); cranial nerve palsies (facial → IX/X/XI, may be permanent); meningitis, intracranial/brain abscess, dural venous sinus thrombosis; and death (mortality remains significant even with treatment).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the key clinical rule for suspecting MOE?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Ordinary otitis externa not improving in a diabetic → think MOE.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is otitis media with effusion (OME/glue ear)?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: A collection of fluid in the middle ear WITHOUT signs of acute infection. It is the commonest cause of acquired (conductive) hearing loss in childhood and the commonest reason for elective surgery in children.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: Why does glue ear matter developmentally?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Persistent hearing loss can cause speech, language, behavioural and educational problems at a critical developmental stage.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the core concept of glue ear?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: It is fluid + hearing loss (NOT infection); most resolve spontaneously (active observation first), and grommets are the key intervention if it persists.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the core mechanism of glue ear?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: The Eustachian tube ventilates/drains the middle ear. If dysfunctional (immature in young children, or blocked by adenoidal hypertrophy or after a URTI/AOM) → negative pressure → transudation of fluid, which becomes thick and 'glue-like' → dampens ossicular movement → conductive hearing loss.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What are the risk factors for glue ear?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Male sex; siblings with glue ear/family history; bottle-feeding (breastfeeding is protective); day-care/nursery attendance (more URTIs); parental smoking (passive smoke); winter/spring season; atopy; and recent AOM/URTI.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: Which two conditions have a much higher prevalence of glue ear and are a special group?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Down syndrome and cleft palate (60–85% prevalence).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: At what age does glue ear peak?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Around 2 years of age.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the presenting feature of glue ear?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Hearing loss (conductive) — which may show as inattention, 'not listening', turning up the TV, speech/language delay, or poor school performance. It is the commonest cause of conductive hearing loss and of elective surgery in children.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What secondary problems can glue ear cause?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Speech and language delay, behavioural problems, and balance problems.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What features are usually ABSENT in glue ear, distinguishing it from AOM?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Usually no pain, fever or discharge — this is fluid, not acute infection (AOM has a bulging red drum, pain and fever).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What are the otoscopy findings in glue ear?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Fluid visible behind an intact tympanic membrane — a dull/retracted drum, sometimes with air-fluid levels or bubbles and loss of the light reflex. There is NO discharge, NO bulging, and NO marked redness (those suggest AOM).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What does tympanometry show in glue ear?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: A flat ('type B') trace (no middle-ear compliance) — confirming an effusion.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What audiometry is done in glue ear?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Age-appropriate pure-tone audiometry — documents the conductive hearing loss and its severity.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: Before acting on a child's glue ear, how many times and over what interval must it be confirmed?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: On 2 occasions ~6–12 weeks apart (as many resolve spontaneously).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the key referral rule for a UNILATERAL OME in an ADULT?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: ALL adults with unilateral OME → 2-week-wait referral — a one-sided adult effusion can be caused by a postnasal space tumour (nasopharyngeal carcinoma) obstructing the Eustachian tube.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: Which children with glue ear should be referred DIRECTLY (no active observation)?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Children with Down syndrome or cleft palate — they need specialist/audiology surveillance; active observation is NOT appropriate.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: When should a child with glue ear be referred?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: With persistent significant hearing loss confirmed on 2 separate occasions (6–12 weeks apart); earlier if there is significant developmental/social/educational impact; and directly if Down syndrome/cleft palate.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the first-line management of glue ear?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Active observation for ~3 months (most resolve spontaneously); auto-inflation (Otovent balloon) can be considered during observation.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What non-surgical option exists for persistent glue ear, and which treatments are NOT recommended?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Hearing aids (an alternative to surgery, especially if surgery is declined/contraindicated). Antibiotics, decongestants, antihistamines and steroids are NOT recommended (ineffective).

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the key surgical treatment for glue ear, and how long do the tubes last?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Grommets (ventilation tubes) inserted into the tympanic membrane to ventilate the middle ear (doing the Eustachian tube's job); most extrude after ~10 months. Risks: perforation, tympanosclerosis, infection/discharge.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: What is the role of adenoidectomy in glue ear, and when is it avoided?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: An adjunct to grommets (removes adenoidal obstruction) — avoided if there is a palate abnormality, as it can worsen velopharyngeal function in cleft palate.

conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).front: Why are antibiotics/decongestants/antihistamines/steroids not used in glue ear?
conditions__ENT__Otitis (Ear Infections).back: Because they are ineffective — glue ear is a non-infective effusion, so it does not respond to these.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is the organising principle for neck lumps?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: By age and site. Causes span congenital (branchial cyst — lateral; thyroglossal — midline, moves with tongue protrusion; dermoid — midline), inflammatory (reactive nodes), and neoplastic (lymphoma, metastatic SCC, salivary tumours). A persistent adult neck lump is cancer until proven otherwise.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is the commonest cause of a neck lump overall?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Reactive lymphadenopathy.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is the triage logic for neck lumps by age?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: In children/young adults, lumps are usually congenital or inflammatory. In adults >40 with a persistent lump, assume malignancy (metastatic SCC or lymphoma) until proven otherwise.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: Classify neck lumps by midline vs lateral location.
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Midline: thyroglossal cyst, dermoid cyst, thyroid nodule/goitre. Lateral: branchial cyst, cystic hygroma, reactive/malignant lymphadenopathy, carotid body tumour, pharyngeal pouch.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is a thyroglossal cyst and its classic sign?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: The commonest congenital midline neck cyst — a persisting thyroglossal duct (the track the thyroid leaves descending from the foramen caecum at the tongue base). Midline, mobile, non-tender, soft, fluctuant. Classic sign: moves upwards on tongue protrusion (and swallowing) — OSCE gold is to ask the patient to stick their tongue out.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What investigation and management apply to a thyroglossal cyst?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: USS/CT; check thyroid function/imaging (the cyst may contain the only functioning thyroid). Management: Sistrunk procedure (excises the cyst + central hyoid + duct tract to prevent recurrence).

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is a branchial cyst and its features?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: A lateral cyst from failure of obliteration of the 2nd branchial cleft — oval, mobile, non-tender, cystic, anterior to sternocleidomastoid, near the angle of the mandible. Presents in teens/early adulthood; may enlarge/infect. Aspirate shows cholesterol crystals ('branCHial = CHolesterol').

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is the important caveat about a 'branchial cyst' in an adult >40?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: It may be a cystic metastasis from a head-and-neck SCC — do USS-guided FNA before excision.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is a dermoid cyst and how is it distinguished from a thyroglossal cyst?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: A midline cyst from ectodermal tissue trapped during embryonic fusion, containing skin appendages (keratin, hair, sebaceous material) — typically midline (submental/floor of mouth), soft, non-tender. Key distinguisher: a dermoid does NOT move with tongue protrusion (unlike a thyroglossal cyst).

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What are the features of reactive lymphadenopathy?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: The commonest cause of a neck lump; follows recent local/viral infection; tender, mobile nodes that settle in 2–6 weeks.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What are the features of lymphoma as a neck lump?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Rubbery, painless nodes; B symptoms (night sweats, fever, weight loss); may be generalised.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is a cystic hygroma?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: A congenital lymphatic malformation, classically in the left neck; ~90% present by age 2; it transilluminates ('cystic hyGLOWma').

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What are the features of a carotid body tumour?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: A pulsatile lateral mass that moves side-to-side but NOT vertically; no movement on swallowing; a bruit may be present.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is a pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's) and who gets it?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Herniation at Killian's dehiscence (between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus), in older men; gurgles on palpation; causes dysphagia, regurgitation, aspiration and chronic cough.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What are the features of a lipoma in the neck?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Soft, non-tender, mobile, with no skin changes — a benign fat tumour; reassure.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: How does a thyroid nodule/goitre move, and how does this distinguish it from a thyroglossal cyst?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: A thyroid lump moves UP on swallowing (not on tongue protrusion); a thyroglossal cyst moves on tongue protrusion. (Moves with tongue protrusion → thyroglossal; moves with swallowing but not tongue protrusion → thyroid.)

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What are the red flags for malignancy in a neck lump?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: A persistent lump >3 weeks in an adult (especially >45); a hard, fixed, non-tender node; associated hoarseness/voice change, dysphagia, odynophagia, referred otalgia, unexplained weight loss, or a mouth/throat ulcer. Risk factors: smoking, alcohol, betel nut, HPV.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What referral does an unexplained adult neck lump warrant?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: An urgent (2-week-wait) suspected head-and-neck cancer referral (NICE NG12).

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is the first-line imaging for a neck lump, and the key cytology test?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Ultrasound (cystic vs solid, nodes, thyroid) is first-line imaging. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC), usually USS-guided, is key for solid/suspicious lumps.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: Why is FNA inadequate if lymphoma is suspected?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: FNA can't subtype lymphoma — it needs architecture, so a core or excisional biopsy is required.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What further investigations are used when malignancy is suspected in a neck lump?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: CT/MRI for staging; nasendoscopy/panendoscopy to find a primary if metastatic SCC is suspected; and bloods (FBC, ± viral serology, LDH if lymphoma; thyroid function for thyroid lesions).

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What does salivary gland disease cover, and why does anatomy matter?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Inflammation, obstruction (stones), and tumours. Anatomy predicts pathology (tumours favour the parotid, stones the submandibular), and the crucial skill is spotting red flags for malignancy — especially facial nerve involvement.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What are the three salivary gland pairs and their predominant pathology?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Parotid (anterior + inferior to the ear) — most tumours (but most parotid tumours are benign). Submandibular (below the angle of the jaw) — most stones (~80%). Sublingual (beneath the tongue) — rare tumours, but a higher % are malignant.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: Why does a facial nerve palsy with a parotid lump mean malignancy until proven otherwise?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Because the facial nerve (CN VII) passes through the parotid gland (dividing it into superficial + deep lobes), so a benign tumour spares it — facial nerve involvement implies infiltration by malignancy. Parotid surgery also risks facial nerve damage.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is the 'rule of 80s' for salivary tumours?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: ~80% of salivary tumours are in the parotid; ~80% of parotid tumours are benign; ~80% of benign parotid tumours are pleomorphic adenomas. (And the smaller the gland, the higher the proportion malignant.)

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: How do salivary tumour, stone, and sialadenitis differ in story?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Tumour: persistent, painless lump (facial nerve palsy → malignant). Stone/obstruction: pain + swelling worse on eating, recurrent, mealtime-related, palpable stone (submandibular). Sialadenitis: acute, painful, swollen gland, often unwell, purulent discharge from the duct.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is a pleomorphic adenoma?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: The commonest salivary gland tumour (typically 40–60 years) — a slow-growing, painless, mobile parotid lump. Management: surgical excision (superficial parotidectomy — risk of CN VII damage). Do NOT enucleate (recurrence). Small risk of malignant transformation → carcinoma ex-pleomorphic adenoma.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is a Warthin's tumour (adenolymphoma)?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: The 2nd commonest benign salivary tumour — in middle-aged males, strongly linked to smoking; almost exclusively parotid; can be bilateral; softer, more mobile, fluctuant/cystic (vs the firmer pleomorphic adenoma).

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is the commonest salivary gland MALIGNANCY?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (especially parotid).

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is notable about adenoid cystic carcinoma?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: It is notorious for perineural invasion (causing pain and facial nerve involvement) and late distant spread.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What are the red flags for a malignant salivary tumour?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Rapid growth, pain, a hard/fixed lump, facial nerve palsy, cervical lymphadenopathy, and skin fixation/ulceration.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is sialolithiasis and its classic symptom?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Salivary gland stones — causing recurrent unilateral pain + swelling on eating (saliva is stimulated but can't drain past the stone).

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: Why are ~80% of salivary stones submandibular?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Because Wharton's duct runs 'uphill' and its saliva is thick/mucinous, making it prone to stones.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What complications can salivary stones cause?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Infection → sialadenitis, and rarely spread (Ludwig's angina — floor-of-mouth cellulitis, an airway emergency).

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: How are salivary stones investigated and managed?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Ix: plain X-ray, sialography, ultrasound; non-contrast CT is sensitive. Mx: conservative (hydration, sialogogues e.g. lemon/sour sweets, gland massage, warm compresses); stone removal (endoscopic sialendoscopy or surgery); gland excision if recurrent.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is sialadenitis and its cardinal sign?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Inflammation/infection of a salivary gland, often secondary to obstruction by a stone — with purulent discharge from the duct (a foul taste in the mouth).

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What are the causes of sialadenitis?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Acute bacterial (commonly Staph aureus, ascending from the mouth — often dehydrated/elderly patients); viral (mumps — bilateral parotid swelling); chronic/autoimmune (recurrent — Sjögren's syndrome, IgG4-related disease).

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: How is sialadenitis managed?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Hydration, analgesia, oral hygiene, antibiotics for bacterial infection; treat the underlying obstruction; and drain any abscess.

conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.front: What is the general investigation approach for salivary gland disease?
conditions__ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary G.back: Ultrasound first-line (cystic vs solid, stones, gland structure); FNAC for tumours (± US-guided); MRI for best soft-tissue characterisation + staging (deep lobe, perineural spread); sialography/CT for stones; and bloods (autoimmune screen if Sjögren's suspected).

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: How is hearing loss classified, and what localises the lesion?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: As conductive (outer/middle ear) or sensorineural (cochlea/nerve). Weber & Rinne plus audiometry localise the lesion.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What are the Weber/Rinne patterns for conductive vs sensorineural loss?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: Conductive (wax, otosclerosis, effusion): Rinne negative (BC > AC), Weber to the affected ear. Sensorineural (presbycusis, SNHL): Rinne positive (AC > BC), Weber to the better ear.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: Name the common causes of hearing loss by type.
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: SNHL: sudden sensorineural hearing loss (emergency), presbycusis (age-related, high-frequency, bilateral). Conductive: otosclerosis (young adult, FHx, stapes fixation), impacted ear wax. Tinnitus is a symptom (exclude unilateral/acoustic neuroma and pulsatile/vascular).

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: Which hearing loss presentation is an emergency, and what does unilateral tinnitus/SNHL warrant?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an ENT emergency — same-day audiometry + high-dose steroids. Unilateral tinnitus/SNHL warrants MRI to exclude an acoustic neuroma.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What is sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL)?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: A rapid-onset sensorineural hearing loss developing over ≤72 hours, unexplained by other causes — a true otological emergency. Hearing loss becomes permanent if not treated early, yet with prompt steroids ~half of patients recover, so the window is short.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What is the audiometric diagnostic criterion for SSNHL?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: A loss of ≥30 dB across 3 consecutive (contiguous) frequencies, developing over ≤72 hours with no other explanation.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What is the first bedside job in suspected SSNHL, and why?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: To prove it is sensorineural, not conductive (Weber/Rinne + otoscopy) — a sudden conductive loss (wax, effusion) is NOT this emergency. SSNHL is a cochlea/CN VIII problem.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What are the typical accompanying symptoms of SSNHL?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: It is often unilateral and may be accompanied by tinnitus and/or vertigo/aural fullness; it may be permanent.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What proportion of SSNHL is idiopathic, and what is the presumed mechanism?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: Most (~85–90%) is idiopathic — presumed viral/vascular/autoimmune.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: List the identifiable causes of SSNHL.
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: Infective (viral — mumps, HSV, VZV; meningitis, syphilis, Lyme); neurological (acoustic neuroma, MS, migraine, stroke — AICA territory); otological (Ménière's); ototoxic drugs; autoimmune/inflammatory (Cogan's syndrome, autoimmune inner-ear disease, vasculitis); and trauma/barotrauma/perilymph fistula.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What is the highest-yield 'don't miss' cause of unilateral SSNHL?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: An acoustic neuroma — a sudden unilateral SNHL, especially with tinnitus/imbalance, must have an acoustic neuroma excluded.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What is the ototoxic-drug mnemonic 'FAV Q&A'?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: Furosemide, Aminoglycosides, Vancomycin, Quinine/NSAIDs, Aspirin — drugs that can cause sensorineural hearing loss.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What does the history in SSNHL need to cover?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: Onset/timescale (≤72 h), uni- vs bilateral, associated tinnitus/vertigo/aural fullness, preceding illness, drugs, trauma, and neurological symptoms.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What should otoscopy and tuning-fork tests show in SSNHL?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: Otoscopy is normal (excludes wax/effusion/perforation). Weber lateralises to the unaffected (better) ear; Rinne is positive (AC > BC) bilaterally — confirming sensorineural loss.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: Why is a neurological examination important in SSNHL?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: To assess cranial nerves (especially V, VII, VIII) and cerebellar signs — looking for a posterior circulation stroke or cerebellopontine angle lesion.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What is the definitive diagnostic investigation for SSNHL?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: Pure-tone audiometry — establishes/confirms the diagnosis (documents the ≥30 dB loss over 3 consecutive frequencies).

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What imaging is done in SSNHL and why?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: MRI of the internal auditory meatus (IAM) — to exclude an acoustic neuroma/retrocochlear pathology (done in all cases), ± stroke/demyelination assessment.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What bloods and other tests may be done in SSNHL?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: As guided: FBC, ESR/CRP, autoimmune screen, syphilis serology, glucose (diabetes = risk/poor prognostic factor); and tympanometry to confirm a normal middle ear.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What is the first-line treatment for SSNHL, and the key timing rule?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: High-dose oral corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone, tapering) for all cases — started as early as possible (best in the first 2 weeks; little benefit beyond ~6 weeks). Refer to ENT immediately (within 24 hours) and don't wait for the MRI to start treatment.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What is intratympanic steroid therapy used for in SSNHL?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: Salvage therapy (if oral steroids fail/are incomplete), or as primary therapy where systemic steroids are contraindicated (e.g. diabetes).

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What adjunct therapy may be used in SSNHL in some centres?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: Hyperbaric oxygen — within ~2 weeks (or salvage within a month).

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What other management applies in SSNHL?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: Treat the underlying cause if identified (antivirals/antibiotics for infection, manage demyelination/Ménière's, stop ototoxic drugs); and audiology follow-up with repeat audiometry and hearing aids/rehabilitation if the loss is permanent.

conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.front: What is the prognosis of SSNHL?
conditions__ENT__Hearing Loss.back: About 50–65% recover some hearing, often within the first 2 weeks.
