A visible bleeding point on the anterior septum
conditions__ENT__Epistaxis Management.answer: Blood trickling down the throat/posterior pharynx with profuse, hard-to-control bleeding
conditions__ENT__Epistaxis Management.explanation: Posterior epistaxis is suggested by profuse, hard-to-control bleeding with blood trickling into the throat (seen on examining the posterior pharynx), typically in older, hypertensive or anticoagulated patients. Anterior bleeds have a visible septal source, are usually milder, and often stop with first aid.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: A 45-year-old man has a 6-month history of foul-smelling discharge from one ear that has not resolved despite several courses of antibiotics, with unilateral hearing loss. Otoscopy shows whitish crusting in the attic (pars flaccida). What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: Persistent foul-smelling otorrhoea unresponsive to antibiotics, unilateral hearing loss, and attic (pars flaccida) crusting/debris are classic for cholesteatoma. Any crusting obscuring the attic is a cholesteatoma until proven otherwise. It needs ENT referral, CT temporal bone and surgery — antibiotics will not cure it.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: What is the definitive treatment of a cholesteatoma?
options: A prolonged course of oral antibiotics
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: Cholesteatoma does not resolve with antibiotics or observation and must be surgically excised — mastoidectomy ± tympanoplasty removes it and reconstructs the eardrum/hearing where possible. Topical antibiotics/aural toilet only control infection peri-operatively and are not curative.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: Which investigation confirms a cholesteatoma and maps its extent/bony erosion before surgery?
options: High-resolution CT of the temporal bone
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.answer: High-resolution CT of the temporal bone
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: High-resolution CT of the temporal bone confirms the diagnosis and maps the extent and bony erosion (ossicles, mastoid, facial canal, tegmen) before surgery. Diffusion-weighted MRI is used mainly to detect residual/recurrent disease after surgery; audiometry documents the hearing loss.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: A patient with a known cholesteatoma develops vertigo when pressure is applied to the tragus. What complication does this suggest?
options: A labyrinthine fistula from erosion into the semicircular canals
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.answer: A labyrinthine fistula from erosion into the semicircular canals
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: Vertigo on pressing the tragus (a positive fistula test) suggests a labyrinthine fistula, where the cholesteatoma has eroded into the labyrinth/semicircular canals. This is a 'danger' sign of local expansion, along with facial nerve palsy and pain, indicating an unsafe ear needing urgent surgery.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: Which type of hearing loss is characteristically caused by cholesteatoma?
options: Unilateral conductive hearing loss (from ossicular erosion)
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.answer: Unilateral conductive hearing loss (from ossicular erosion)
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: Cholesteatoma typically causes unilateral conductive hearing loss from erosion of the ossicles. Sensorineural loss can also occur if it erodes into the inner ear (a danger sign), but the characteristic picture is progressive unilateral conductive loss with foul discharge.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: A child is found to have a pearly white mass behind an intact eardrum, with no history of ear discharge or perforation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: A pearly white mass behind an INTACT eardrum in a child with no discharge or perforation is a congenital cholesteatoma (a rest of embryonic epithelium). Acquired cholesteatoma instead arises from a retraction pocket or perforation and presents with foul discharge and attic debris.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: Which statement about the pathophysiology of primary acquired cholesteatoma is correct?
options: Eustachian tube dysfunction causes negative pressure and a pars flaccida retraction pocket, which traps keratin into an expanding, bone-eroding sac
It is a malignant tumour of the middle ear
It results from excess cholesterol deposition
It is caused by ossicular overgrowth
It is a viral infection of the eardrum
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.answer: Eustachian tube dysfunction causes negative pressure and a pars flaccida retraction pocket, which traps keratin into an expanding, bone-eroding sac
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: Primary acquired cholesteatoma arises from Eustachian tube dysfunction → negative middle-ear pressure → a pars flaccida (attic) retraction pocket that can no longer self-clean → trapped keratin forms an expanding sac that releases enzymes and gets infected, eroding bone. It is benign but locally destructive, and contains no cholesterol/fat.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: A patient with a longstanding cholesteatoma develops fever, severe headache and neck stiffness. What life-threatening complication must be considered?
options: Intracranial complication such as meningitis or brain abscess
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.answer: Intracranial complication such as meningitis or brain abscess
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: Cholesteatoma can erode into the cranial cavity and cause life-threatening intracranial complications — meningitis, brain abscess, and sigmoid/lateral sinus thrombosis. Fever, severe headache and neck stiffness suggest meningitis, requiring emergency assessment. This is why cholesteatoma is the classic 'unsafe' ear disease.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: On otoscopy, crusting and wax are obscuring the attic (pars flaccida) of the eardrum. What is the correct clinical approach?
options: Reassure — attic crusting is always benign wax
Ignore it if hearing is normal
Treat as a possible cholesteatoma until proven otherwise, and arrange proper examination/microsuction to see behind it
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.answer: Treat as a possible cholesteatoma until proven otherwise, and arrange proper examination/microsuction to see behind it
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: The clinical rule is that any crusting/wax obscuring the attic (pars flaccida) is a cholesteatoma until proven otherwise, so it must be properly examined (microsuction) to visualise behind it. Missing a cholesteatoma risks progressive bone erosion and dangerous complications.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: A patient with a cholesteatoma develops weakness of one side of the face. Which structure has most likely been eroded?
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: Facial weakness in cholesteatoma indicates erosion of the facial nerve canal, causing a facial nerve palsy — a 'danger' sign of local destruction requiring urgent surgery. Other danger signs include vertigo (labyrinthine fistula) and pain.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: Why are topical antibiotics and aural toilet used in cholesteatoma even though they are not curative?
options: They replace the need for surgery
They control active infection and discharge peri-operatively, but surgery remains definitive
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.answer: They control active infection and discharge peri-operatively, but surgery remains definitive
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: Topical antibiotics and aural toilet (microsuction) control active infection and discharge around the time of surgery, improving the operative field and symptoms, but they do not remove the keratinising epithelium — surgery is the only definitive treatment. Cholesteatoma will recur/persist without excision.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: After surgery for cholesteatoma, which investigation is most useful for detecting residual or recurrent disease?
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: Diffusion-weighted MRI is the investigation of choice for detecting residual or recurrent cholesteatoma after surgery, as recurrence/residual rates are high (~20–30%). CT is used pre-operatively to map extent and bony erosion; audiometry documents hearing.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: Which of the following best explains why cholesteatoma is described as 'benign but locally destructive'?
options: It is a slow-growing cancer that metastasises
It only affects the skin of the external ear
It is not a cancer, but it erodes surrounding bone (ossicles, facial canal, labyrinth, skull base) as it expands
It is destructive only if malignant transformation occurs
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.answer: It is not a cancer, but it erodes surrounding bone (ossicles, facial canal, labyrinth, skull base) as it expands
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: Cholesteatoma is not a neoplasm (benign), but the expanding keratin sac releases bone-destroying enzymes and becomes repeatedly infected, eroding the ossicles, facial nerve canal, labyrinth, mastoid and even the skull base — hence 'locally destructive' and the source of its dangerous complications.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: A patient with chronic ear discharge is found to have a retraction pocket in the pars flaccida with accumulating debris. Which type of cholesteatoma is this?
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: A retraction pocket in the pars flaccida (attic) accumulating keratin debris is the mechanism of PRIMARY acquired cholesteatoma. Secondary acquired cholesteatoma follows direct injury/perforation of the eardrum, and congenital cholesteatoma occurs behind an intact drum with no discharge.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: Which feature would prompt urgent ENT referral in a patient with suspected cholesteatoma?
options: Mild wax in the ear canal
Foul-smelling discharge unresponsive to antibiotics with attic debris, hearing loss, vertigo or facial weakness
A single episode of earache that resolved
Bilateral symmetrical hearing loss with no discharge
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.answer: Foul-smelling discharge unresponsive to antibiotics with attic debris, hearing loss, vertigo or facial weakness
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: Persistent foul-smelling discharge unresponsive to antibiotics, attic debris/crusting, conductive hearing loss, and any danger signs (vertigo, facial weakness) warrant urgent ENT referral for microsuction, CT and surgery. Cholesteatoma is progressive and can cause serious complications if not treated.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: Which statement about the difference between canal-wall-up and canal-wall-down mastoidectomy is correct?
options: Canal-wall-down preserves canal anatomy but has higher recurrence
Canal-wall-up is only used in children
Canal-wall-up preserves canal anatomy but has higher recurrence; canal-wall-down leaves an open mastoid cavity with lower recurrence
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.answer: Canal-wall-up preserves canal anatomy but has higher recurrence; canal-wall-down leaves an open mastoid cavity with lower recurrence
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: Canal-wall-up mastoidectomy preserves the ear canal anatomy but carries a higher recurrence rate, whereas canal-wall-down creates an open mastoid cavity with a lower recurrence rate. The choice depends on the extent of disease, and both aim to fully remove the cholesteatoma.

conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.question: A patient asks why their persistent smelly ear discharge keeps coming back despite repeated antibiotic drops. What is the best explanation?
options: A cholesteatoma (trapped, infected keratin) may be present, which antibiotics cannot cure — it needs surgical removal
The antibiotics are the wrong class
The ear canal is too dry
It is simple wax that will clear itself
It is an allergy to the drops
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.answer: A cholesteatoma (trapped, infected keratin) may be present, which antibiotics cannot cure — it needs surgical removal
conditions__ENT__Cholesteatoma.explanation: Persistent, recurrent foul-smelling discharge unresponsive to antibiotics is a red flag for cholesteatoma, where trapped infected keratin cannot be eradicated by antibiotics. Definitive treatment is surgical removal, so the patient needs ENT referral, examination of the attic, and CT imaging.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: A 48-year-old has recurrent attacks of severe rotational vertigo lasting about an hour, each with nausea, ringing and a sense of fullness in the left ear, and fluctuating hearing loss on that side. Between attacks she is well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: Ménière's disease
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Episodic vertigo lasting minutes–hours with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness is the classic tetrad of Ménière's disease (endolymphatic hydrops).

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: What is the underlying pathophysiological abnormality in Ménière's disease?
options: Endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph in the membranous labyrinth)
Otoconia displaced into a semicircular canal
A vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle
Reactivation of varicella-zoster in the geniculate ganglion
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: Endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph in the membranous labyrinth)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Ménière's disease is caused by endolymphatic hydrops — excess endolymph distending the membranous labyrinth, disrupting cochlear and vestibular function.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: A 60-year-old has brief spells of vertigo lasting under a minute, triggered each time by rolling over in bed or looking up, with no hearing loss or tinnitus. Which diagnosis is most likely?
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Brief, positionally triggered vertigo lasting seconds with no hearing loss is BPPV; Dix-Hallpike is positive and the Epley manoeuvre is the treatment.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: A patient has acute, constant vertigo lasting several days after a recent viral upper respiratory infection, with no hearing loss or tinnitus. Which diagnosis fits best?
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: Vestibular neuronitis
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Prolonged (days) acute vertigo after a viral illness without hearing loss is vestibular neuronitis; adding hearing loss would make it labyrinthitis.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: A patient with acute vertigo has the HINTS examination performed. Which finding is reassuringly peripheral (e.g. consistent with a vestibular cause rather than a stroke)?
options: A normal head impulse test with direction-changing nystagmus
An abnormal head impulse test (corrective saccade), unidirectional horizontal nystagmus and no skew deviation
A normal head impulse with skew deviation
Gaze-evoked nystagmus in all directions with limb ataxia
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: An abnormal head impulse test (corrective saccade), unidirectional horizontal nystagmus and no skew deviation
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: A peripheral pattern is an abnormal head impulse (corrective saccade), unidirectional horizontal nystagmus and no skew; a normal head impulse or skew/direction-changing nystagmus suggests a central cause.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: A patient with acute vertigo also has limb ataxia, diplopia and a normal head impulse test. What must be urgently excluded?
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: A posterior circulation (brainstem/cerebellar) stroke
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Persistent vertigo with other neurology (ataxia, diplopia) and a normal head impulse points to a central cause — a posterior circulation stroke must be excluded.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: Which investigation is most useful to confirm and characterise the hearing loss of Ménière's disease?
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: Pure-tone audiometry
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Audiometry confirms a sensorineural pattern of hearing loss (typically low-frequency and fluctuating early), the key test in Ménière's disease.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: A patient with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and episodic vertigo is referred. Why is an MRI often arranged?
options: To exclude an acoustic neuroma and central causes
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: To exclude an acoustic neuroma and central causes
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: MRI is used to exclude an acoustic neuroma (a cause of unilateral SNHL) and central pathology before settling on a diagnosis of Ménière's disease.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: What is the most appropriate treatment for an acute attack of Ménière's vertigo with vomiting?
options: A short course of a vestibular sedative such as prochlorperazine (or an antihistamine like cyclizine)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: A short course of a vestibular sedative such as prochlorperazine (or an antihistamine like cyclizine)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Acute attacks are managed with short-term vestibular sedatives/antiemetics (prochlorperazine, cyclizine, cinnarizine); prophylaxis (betahistine) is a longer-term measure.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: Which combination is first-line for reducing the frequency of Ménière's attacks?
options: Betahistine plus a low-salt diet (± reduced caffeine/alcohol)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: Betahistine plus a low-salt diet (± reduced caffeine/alcohol)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Prophylaxis is betahistine (first-line) with lifestyle measures (low-salt diet, reduced caffeine/alcohol); diuretics are sometimes added.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: A patient with disabling Ménière's disease refractory to medical therapy is offered intratympanic gentamicin. What is the key risk to counsel about?
options: Ototoxicity with a risk of hearing loss (it ablates vestibular function)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: Ototoxicity with a risk of hearing loss (it ablates vestibular function)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Intratympanic gentamicin ablates vestibular function but is ototoxic, carrying a risk of hearing loss — an important counselling point in refractory disease.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: What specific driving advice should be given to a patient with active Ménière's disease?
options: They must inform the DVLA and stop driving during active disease until symptoms are controlled
No advice is needed as it does not affect driving
They may drive as long as they carry medication
They are permanently banned from driving
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: They must inform the DVLA and stop driving during active disease until symptoms are controlled
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Because of sudden, unpredictable vertigo, patients must inform the DVLA and stop driving during active disease until symptoms are controlled.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: A patient with long-standing Ménière's disease describes sudden falls to the ground without warning or loss of consciousness. What is this feature called?
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: Tumarkin crises (drop attacks)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Sudden falls without warning (drop attacks) in later Ménière's disease are Tumarkin crises, thought to arise from sudden otolithic dysfunction.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: A patient has brief, seconds-long spinning triggered by rolling over in bed, with no hearing loss. Which condition is most likely?
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: BPPV
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Seconds-long positional vertigo with no hearing loss is BPPV (diagnosed with Dix-Hallpike, treated with Epley).

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: A patient has episodic vertigo lasting minutes to hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness. Which condition is this?
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: Ménière's disease
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Episodic vertigo with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness is Ménière's disease.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: A patient has several days of constant vertigo after a viral illness, WITHOUT hearing loss. Which condition is this?
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: Vestibular neuritis
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Days of constant post-viral vertigo without hearing loss is vestibular neuritis (labyrinthitis would add hearing loss).

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: Which feature should prompt urgent imaging for a central cause of vertigo?
options: New neurology, direction-changing nystagmus, a normal head-impulse test or a new headache
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: New neurology, direction-changing nystagmus, a normal head-impulse test or a new headache
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Central features (other neurology, gaze-evoked/direction-changing nystagmus, normal head-impulse test, new headache) warrant urgent imaging for posterior-circulation stroke.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: What is the most useful framework for approaching a patient with vertigo?
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: Duration + trigger + associated features
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Vertigo is best approached by duration, trigger and associated features, which point to BPPV, neuritis or Ménière's, and flag central causes.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: A 60-year-old has brief episodes of spinning lasting about 20 seconds, triggered by rolling over in bed and looking up, with no hearing loss or tinnitus and a normal neuro exam. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Brief positional vertigo with no hearing loss/tinnitus and a normal neuro exam is BPPV.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: What is the underlying mechanism of BPPV?
options: Displaced otoconia (canalithiasis) in a semicircular canal, usually the posterior canal
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: Displaced otoconia (canalithiasis) in a semicircular canal, usually the posterior canal
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: BPPV results from otoconia dislodged from the utricle into a semicircular canal (usually posterior) — canalithiasis.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: Which diagnostic manoeuvre confirms posterior canal BPPV?
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre is the gold-standard diagnostic test for posterior canal BPPV.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: What is a positive Dix-Hallpike response?
options: After a short latency, transient, fatiguable rotational (torsional) upbeating nystagmus with vertigo
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: After a short latency, transient, fatiguable rotational (torsional) upbeating nystagmus with vertigo
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: A positive Dix-Hallpike shows latent, transient, fatiguable torsional-upbeating nystagmus with vertigo.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: What is the treatment of choice for posterior canal BPPV?
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: The Epley manoeuvre (canalith repositioning)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: The Epley manoeuvre (canalith repositioning) is the treatment of choice, >90% effective.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: Why should vestibular sedatives (e.g. prochlorperazine) NOT be used for BPPV?
options: They cause the crystals to reform
They don't treat the mechanical cause and can worsen/prolong it (they are for the acute nausea of neuritis/labyrinthitis)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: They don't treat the mechanical cause and can worsen/prolong it (they are for the acute nausea of neuritis/labyrinthitis)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Vestibular sedatives don't address the mechanical cause of BPPV and may prolong it; they are for acute neuritis/labyrinthitis nausea.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: Which feature would suggest a CENTRAL cause rather than BPPV?
options: Vertical/bidirectional nystagmus, ataxia or cranial nerve signs
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: Vertical/bidirectional nystagmus, ataxia or cranial nerve signs
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Vertical/bidirectional nystagmus, ataxia or CN signs point to a central cause (e.g. posterior circulation stroke), warranting imaging.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: In the HINTS exam for acute persistent vertigo, which finding is reassuring (peripheral)?
options: An ABNORMAL head impulse test (a corrective saccade)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: An ABNORMAL head impulse test (a corrective saccade)
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: Counterintuitively, an abnormal head impulse test (corrective saccade) is reassuring/peripheral; a normal head impulse with vertical nystagmus/skew suggests a central cause.

conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.question: Which feature best distinguishes BPPV from Ménière's disease and labyrinthitis?
options: The ABSENCE of hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness in BPPV
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.answer: The ABSENCE of hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness in BPPV
conditions__ENT__Vertigo & Balance Disor.explanation: BPPV has no hearing loss, tinnitus or aural fullness — a key discriminator from Ménière's disease and labyrinthitis.
